s: Specific learning disorder in mathematics
x: dyscalculia specific learning disorder in mathematics persistent difficulty with number sense: comparing quantities, estimating results, seeing without counting that 9 is bigger than 7. 2 counts on their fingers long after classmates have automatised basic mental arithmetic. 2 , 3 does not retain number facts (times tables) despite repeated practice — every calculation starts from scratch. 3 gets lost in multi-step problems even when they understand the concept; swaps or forgets intermediate steps. 4 performance in mathematics clearly below what verbal reasoning and other subjects would predict. 1 it is not "being bad at maths" or a lack of study: it is a specific learning disorder with a neurobiological basis, just as dyslexia is for reading. 1 , 2 it is not maths anxiety, although the two feed each other: anxiety worsens performance, but dyscalculia exists independently of it. 3 it does not go away with more of the same exercises: it improves with explicit, structured intervention on number sense, not with repetition of what has already failed. 4 keep concrete materials and visual representations (number lines, blocks, diagrams) available without stigma — the move from concrete to abstract happens in explicit stages. 4 allow a number-facts table or a calculator when calculation is not the point of the task — assess reasoning separately from arithmetic. reduce the load: fewer, well-chosen exercises with extended time — speed is not the goal. say the steps out loud and leave a worked example visible during the task — explicit instruction, with modelling. 4 separate mathematics from intelligence from the outset: "the reasoning is intact — the difficulty is specific to numbers". explain that supports such as a calculator or a printed times table are not "going easy on them": they are the equivalent of glasses for someone who cannot see at a distance. suggest short, concrete practice at home (board games with dice, real money while shopping) instead of lists of repeated exercises. bear in mind that dyscalculia is heritable and far less well known than dyslexia: the family may never have heard the term — naming the pattern helps. 3 self-concept declining specifically around mathematics ("i'm stupid with numbers"). avoidance or refusal of tasks involving numbers to the point of compromising their school path. persistent discrepancy between general reasoning and mathematical performance without a formal assessment — refer for psychopedagogical assessment. 1 frequently overlaps with dyslexia — the phonological and numerical deficits coexist — and with adhd, where an overloaded working memory makes calculation worse. when reading and numbers fail together, adaptations must cover both fronts, not pick one. american psychiatric s: Specific learning disorder in reading

not respond to repeated correction. 1 tends to avoid reading aloud; may look like disinterest when it is, in fact, a protective strategy. oral comprehension clearly higher than reading comprehension — the difficulty is specific, not a general cognitive limitation. 1 it is not a lack of intelligence: by definition, dyslexia is unexpected relative to the student’s other cognitive abilities. 1 it is not a vision problem or simply “mixing up letters”: the core deficit is in phonological processing. 2 , 3 it is not “cured” , but structured intervention in phonological awareness and decoding improves reading consistently. 2 , 3 increase letter and line spacing: there is experimental evidence that wider spacing improves reading in dyslexic children, with no prior training. 4 evidence for special “dyslexia” fonts is, by contrast, weaker and inconsistent. allow silent reading before any reading aloud — never ask a student to read without warning. when the aim is not to assess writing, s: Developmental coordination disorder
x: dyspraxia developmental coordination disorder handwriting that is difficult, slow, and often illegible — from genuine motor difficulty, not carelessness. 1 , 2 difficulty with the spatial organisation of the notebook, managing materials, and sequences of steps. 3 may seem "clumsy" — spills cups, bumps into furniture, struggles in sport. 1 disproportionate fatigue after tasks requiring sustained fine motor coordination. cognitive ability is usually intact — hence the frequent frustration between knowing and being able to show it. 1 it is not laziness or a lack of effort. 1 it is not just poor handwriting: the clinical term is developmental coordination disorder (dcd), and it affects planning and motor sequencing, not only writing. 2 , 3 it is not solved by "practising handwriting more": effective intervention is task-oriented, not rote repetition. 2 , 4 allow the use of a keyboard/tablet for longer pieces of writing. 2 reduce mechanical copying from the board — provide notes where relevant. 2 provide explicit checklists for multi-step tasks. 3 assess the work by its content, not its physical presentation. 2 explain what dyspraxia is in plain language — most parents/guardians have never heard the term: "it is a neurological difficulty with coordinating movement, not carelessness or a lack of effort". illegible handwriting is the biggest point of friction with parents/guardians — showing that assessment now values content over form helps ease anxiety on both sides. suggest practical tools for home: voice dictation on the phone for notes, a keyboard for longer written work. if there is a history of "he/she is lazy" or "does not try" in previous years, name it directly: "i know you have heard that before — my reading is different". total refusal to produce written work. social isolation in physical-activity contexts. signs of somatised anxiety before written assessments — psychosocial distress is part of the picture. 2 frequently overlaps with adhd and dyslexia; s: English as an Additional Language — student without proficiency in the language of instruction

normal "silent period" in language acquisition, not disinterest. 3 may be exhausted by the end of the day from processing the language in real time. risk of underdiagnosing genuine educational needs (dyslexia, adhd) by attributing everything to the language barrier. 1 it is not a lack of intelligence or ability. 2 it is not merely a matter of time: academic language takes years to develop, and without explicit support many students plateau at a low functional level. 2 it is not solved by automatic translation during the lesson — it is a process of years, and the home language is a resource, bilingual classmate for informal mediation at critical moments. 4 accept early work with grammatical errors — correct content, not form, in the first phase. 3 the meeting itself is a barrier — the s: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
x: adhd attention deficit hyperactivity disorder difficulty sustaining attention on long tasks; gets lost in multi-step instructions. 1 , 2 constant movement — does not stay seated, fidgets, gets up for no apparent reason. 1 answers before the question is finished; interrupts peers and the teacher. 1 , 2 forgets materials, deadlines, and instructions given aloud minutes ago — working memory is overloaded. 2 may hyper-focus on something that interests them, giving the (false) impression that they "could if they wanted to"; in fact, performance varies with interest and reward. 4 it is not bad manners, laziness, or a lack of character: these misconceptions stigmatise and delay support. 3 it is not always visible hyperactivity — there is a predominantly inattentive presentation, more common in girls and often underdiagnosed. 1 , 5 it is not solved by "trying harder": the difficulty lies in neurological self-regulation, not willpower. 2 , 3 break instructions into pieces: one at a time, written on the board, with a set time — this reduces the load on working memory. 2 allow legitimate movement (handing out materials, cleaning the board, running errands). reduce competing stimuli (a seat away from the window, the door, the noisiest group). immediate, frequent positive reinforcement: in adhd, sensitivity to reward is altered (delay aversion), so immediate rewards work better than deferred ones. 4 start with what the student does well — the meeting shouldn't open with a list of complaints, or the parent/guardian becomes defensive. describe observed behaviours, not diagnoses: "when there are more than two steps in a row, they lose the thread" rather than "they have adhd". anticipate the "it is not like this at home" reaction — explain that the group context and the demand for sustained attention in class make the symptoms more visible. if you suggest an assessment, present it as a resource, not a punishment: "there is support that could help them a lot" rather than "they need to be assessed". persistent disciplinary failure despite classroom adaptations. signs of social exclusion by peers. signs of comorbidity (anxiety, depression, oppositional defiant disorder) — common in adhd and warranting referral. 3 adhd rarely comes alone: a substantial share of these students also have a learning disorder — dyslexia and dyscalculia are the most common overlaps, and s: Significantly above-average ability, frequently under-stimulated

s: Assess to learn, not just to grade

s: Decree-Law 573, Law 5378 and the Special Education Services Regulation in Türkiye
x: legal framework türkiye decree-law 573, law 5378 and the special education services regulation in türkiye decree-law 573 ( özel eğitim hakkında kanun hükmünde kararname , 1997) is the founding text: it sets the principles by which individuals requiring special education exercise their right to general and vocational education. 1 law 5378 ( engelliler hakkında kanun , 2005, amended since) covers rights, dignity and equal participation of people with disabilities, education included. 2 the special education services regulation ( özel eğitim hizmetleri yönetmeliği ), republished on 7 july 2018, is the operative text: it governs educational assessment, placement and the day-to-day organisation of support. 3 türkiye ratified the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities in 2009 and its optional protocol in 2015. 5 educational assessment is carried out by the ram ( rehberlik ve araştırma merkezi , guidance and research centre) of the province or district, not by the school. 3 the school opens the process through the guidance service; the referral and the appointment run through the ministry’s mebbi̇s-ram module, and parental involvement is required. 3 the ram’s special education evaluation board decides on placement and on the support the pupil receives. diagnosis belongs to specialist professionals — the teacher’s role is observation and referral. 3 kaynaştırma/bütünleştirme (inclusion through mainstreaming) is the default: the pupil is educated with peers in the general class, with support, rather than separately. 3 every pupil identified as requiring special education has an individualised education programme — the bep ( bireyselleştirilmiş eğitim programı ) — with goals set for the year and reviewed. 3 the bep is drawn up by a team that includes the class teacher and the parents; it is a working document for the classroom, not a file that stays in the office. 3 support may also take the form of a destek eğitim odası (resource room) within the same school, for part of the timetable. 3 bi̇lsem centres ( bilim ve sanat merkezleri ) provide out-of-school provision for gifted pupils and exist in all 81 provinces. 4 identification takes place in grades 1–3 , in three fields: general intellectual ability, visual arts and music. 4 the process starts with the class teacher , who completes the observation form for the pupils nominated, through the school’s guidance commission. 4 founding text: decree-law 573 (1997); operative text: special education services regulation (2018). 1 , 3 assessment and placement: ram, through the school’s guidance service. 3 individual plan: bep, written with the class teacher and the family. 3 gifted provision: bi̇lsem, nominated by the class teacher in grades 1–3. 4 özel eğitim hakkında kanun hükmünde kararname (khk 573), 1997 — mevzuat bilgi sistemi. ↗ engelliler hakkında kanun (kanun no. 5378), 1 july 2005 — mevzuat bilgi sistemi. ↗ özel eğitim hizmetleri yönetmeliği, 7 july 2018 — ministry of national education, directorate general for special education and guidance services. ↗ bilim ve sanat merkezleri öğrenci tanılama ve yerleştirme kılavuzu — ministry of national education. ↗ türkiye’s ratification of the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities — ministry of foreign affairs, press release no. 167, 29 september 2009. ↗

s: The Education Act of 2023, in force since August 2024, and individually adapted education in Norway
x: legal framework norway the education act of 2023, in force since august 2024, and individually adapted education in norway the education act ( opplæringslova , lov-2023-06-09-30) was passed in june 2023 and has applied since 1 august 2024 , replacing the 1998 act. 1 it removes the term spesialundervisning (special education) deliberately: the word was judged stigmatising and to contribute to exclusion. 3 in its place stand three things — individuelt tilrettelagt opplæring (individually adapted education), fysisk tilrettelegging (physical adaptation) and personleg assistanse (personal assistance). 3 chapter 11 governs all of this, and for the first time writes the mandate of the educational-psychological service into the act itself. 1 , 2 tilpassa opplæring — adapting ordinary teaching to the pupils in front of you — is a general duty owed to every pupil. it is not a measure, and it needs no decision. 2 a pupil who cannot get satisfactory benefit from ordinary teaching has a right to individually adapted education (§ 11-6). that does require a formal decision. 1 the pp service ( pedagogisk-psykologisk teneste , ppt) produces the sakkyndig vurdering — the expert assessment a decision must be based on. 1 ppt must assess the pupil’s whole education offering, including the need for physical adaptation and personal assistance — not the teaching alone. 1 worth knowing: under the new act the municipality and ppt weigh more heavily in shaping the provision, and pupils and parents less than before. 3 the school draws up an individuell opplæringsplan (iop) setting out the goals, the content and how the education is to be carried out. 1 once a year the school writes an account of the education the pupil actually received and an assessment of progress against the iop’s goals. 1 central text: opplæringslova (2023), chapter 11 — in force 1 august 2024. 1 right to individually adapted education: § 11-6, on an expert assessment from ppt. 1 individual plan: iop, with a written yearly account. 1 the word “special education” no longer appears in the act. 3 lov om grunnskoleopplæringa og den vidaregåande opplæringa (opplæringslova), lov-2023-06-09-30, kapittel 11 — lovdata. ↗ tilpassa opplæring og individuell tilrettelegging, kap. 11 — statsforvalteren i nordland. ↗ a new education act in norway: a redefinition of special education that nurtures inclusive education? european journal of special needs education . ↗

s: Compulsory School Act No. 91/2008 and Regulation No. 585/2010 on pupils with special needs in Iceland
x: legal framework iceland compulsory school act no. 91/2008 and regulation no. 585/2010 on pupils with special needs in iceland the compulsory school act no. 91/2008 makes education compulsory from six to sixteen and sets inclusive education as the frame. 1 regulation no. 585/2010 on pupils with special needs in compulsory schools applies to pupils who need special educational support according to assessed needs; its stated focus is equality in education. 2 inclusive education — skóli án aðgreiningar , a school without segregation — is the guiding national policy at every level, from early years through the transition to adulthood. 2 the policy addresses every learner’s needs without defining those who need support as a different kind of pupil . 2 the question has been reversed over time: it is no longer inclusion that has to be justified, but the decision to consider a segregated option. 3 under regulation no. 585/2010 the special education teacher draws up the individual education plan and organises the teaching together with the guardians . 3 plans are reviewed at least once a year. 3 this holds at pre-primary, compulsory and upper-secondary level, and in special units inside schools. 3 act no. 86/2021 on the integration of services in the interest of children’s prosperity was passed unanimously and came into force on 1 january 2022. 4 it organises services in three levels and assigns a coordinator to any child needing support, whose job is to keep information, access and continuity from falling between services. 4 implementation is phased and runs to the end of 2026, so practice in a given municipality may still be catching up with the text. 4 central texts: compulsory school act no. 91/2008; regulation no. 585/2010. 1 , 2 individual plan: written by the special education teacher with the guardians, reviewed yearly. 3 cross-service support: prosperity act no. 86/2021, with a named coordinator. 4 compulsory school act no. 91/2008 (english translation) — government of iceland. ↗ iceland: legislation and policy — european agency for special needs and inclusive education. ↗ iceland: systems of support and specialist provision — european agency for special needs and inclusive education. ↗ iceland’s act on the integration of services in the interest of children’s prosperity (“prosperity act”) — oecd. ↗

s: The Law on the Foundations of the Education System and the three levels of the individual education plan in Serbia
x: legal framework serbia the law on the foundations of the education system and the three levels of the individual education plan in serbia the law on the foundations of the education system ( zakon o osnovama sistema obrazovanja i vaspitanja ) was adopted in 2009 and has been amended several times since, including in 2017 and 2025. 1 it commits the system to inclusion and to reasonable accommodation in line with an individual education plan , across primary, secondary and tertiary education. 2 iop1 — adapted programme. adjusted methods, materials, environment and support staff. the learning outcomes themselves are unchanged. 3 iop2 — modified programme. everything in iop1, plus adjusted learning outcomes and content, in one subject, several, or all of them. 3 iop3 — enriched and deepened programme , for pupils with exceptional abilities. gifted pupils sit inside the same instrument rather than outside it — a point worth knowing, because it is unusual. 3 preschools use iop1 only; primary and secondary schools may use all three. 3 the school’s inclusive-education team — specialists, teachers and the parents — proposes the plan. 2 once the right to an iop is accepted, that team proposes who will sit on the pupil’s additional-support team. 3 at municipal level the inter-sectoral committee ( interresorna komisija ) coordinates support across education, health and social services — the mechanism to use when a pupil’s needs cross those boundaries. 1 pedagogical assistants ( pedagoški asistent ) and personal assistants are part of the statutory support, alongside individualised teaching methods and plans. 1 central text: law on the foundations of the education system (2009, as amended). 1 plan: iop1 adapted · iop2 modified outcomes · iop3 enriched, for exceptional ability. 3 proposed by: the school’s inclusive-education team, with the parents on it. 2 across services: the municipal inter-sectoral committee. 1 overview of the inclusive education system in serbia — european agency for special needs and inclusive education. ↗ serbia: legislation and policy — european agency for special needs and inclusive education. ↗ pravilnik o bližim uputstvima za utvrđivanje prava na individualni obrazovni plan, njegovu primenu i vrednovanje — paragraf. ↗

s: The Law on Primary Education (2019) and the Concept for Inclusive Education (2020) in North Macedonia
x: legal framework north macedonia the law on primary education (2019) and the concept for inclusive education (2020) in north macedonia the law on primary education of 2019 is the turning point: it stipulates that children with disabilities are to be enrolled in mainstream education. 1 the concept for inclusive education of 2020 followed as the guideline for putting that into practice at every stage. 2 under the law on primary education and the law on secondary education, an inclusive team is formed for the individual learner and stays with them until they finish primary education. 3 that team prepares and implements the learner’s individual education plan . 3 the reform converted special schools into resource centres and special classes into learning-support centres. 3 a learner with complex needs following a modified curriculum may enrol in a school with a resource centre — on the learner’s or parents’ choice, with professional recommendation. it is a choice, not a placement. 3 educational assistants and physical accessibility became a requirement rather than an aspiration. 3 schools were staffed with special educators, psychologists and pedagogues, supported by teacher training and assistive technology. 2 central texts: law on primary education (2019); concept for inclusive education (2020). 1 , 2 plan: individual education plan, written by the learner’s inclusive team. 3 specialist provision: resource centres (former special schools), entered by choice. 3 north macedonia: new concepts for inclusive education and primary education — eurydice, european commission. ↗ inclusive education in north macedonia — unicef policy brief. ↗ overview of the inclusive education system in north macedonia — european agency for special needs and inclusive education. ↗
